newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Europe soymeal buyers seen playing waiting game.
newsitem.headline: Europe soymeal buyers seen playing waiting game.

text.p: An explosive rally in the Chicago soycomplex this week has left the European physical trade shell-shocked and will heighten consumer reluctance to buy needed mid-protein products, trade sources said on Wednesday.
"The consumers are covered nearby but from May onwards they need soymeal," said Arie van Dijk of market analysts Stigevo.
"But I can't see them doing anything this week with the market in the shape it is."

CBOT soymeal futures ended near the $10 per tonne upper limit on Tuesday after the USDA downwardly revised its quarterly soybean stocks figure. The May soymeal contract peaked at $293.00 per tonne, the highest since 1988.
The USDA corrected its stock total by 22 million bushels, putting the figure at 1.056 billion bushels, down from the 1.078 billion bushel total released on Monday.
Prices then eased on Chicago's Project A trading overnight.
Despite this, European sellers were offering South American soymeal pellets some $10 to $15 higher this morning amid a market wary of price volatility and unsure of future direction.
"Nobody seems to know what will happen next," a broker said.

Van Dijk estimated that for protein products, consumers were around 80 percent covered in April but this dropped drastically further out. Soymeal alternatives such as rapemeal -- already in short supply, and sunflowermeal -- currently at maximum usage -- offered no easy solutions for compounders.
"At some point they will have to come in and buy (soymeal) but at the moment they're betting prices will ease," he said.
Commenting on the USDA revision, traders here said there was little imminent danger to product availability as the Brazilian and Argentine crops would soon be hitting European ports.
One factor on the positive side was that the dollar, easing off its highs, could spark some demand for mid-proteins.
The USDA has predicted this year's soybean plantings would be as high as in the early 1980s and dealers said they expected the new crop to exert a downward influence on prices.

But others cited the possibility of a springtime squeeze, a market factor once quite common but not really in evidence in the past few years. This could force consumers back into the market earlier than anticipated, they said.
